results.title: Scientific models are falsifiable | Science or not?
results.content: # Scientific models are falsifiable. **For a model to be regarded as scientific, there must be some way of testing whether it is false. A model remains in contention as long as no falsifying evidence appears from such tests.**. ## What does it mean for a model to be falsifiable? Scientific models must have the potential to be refuted or falsified. ## How to tell that a model is falsifiable. A scientific model should specify what evidence would falsify it. Most scientific models are presented in a straightforward way, and it’s not difficult to see how they can be falsified. If a model is so vague and all-encompassing that is compatible with all possible evidence, then it cannot be falsifiable. ## Why models must be falsifiable. It may seem paradoxical, but it’s because scientific models are falsifiable that we can have confidence in them. Scientists accept a model when it is supported by evidence, but there is always the possibility that falsifying evidence may be found. Good science, as well as looking for evidence in support of a model (see Scientific models are tested against the real world), actively checks to see whether falsifying evidence exists, . If, as time goes on, supporting evidence accumulates and no falsifying evidence is found, scientists have increasing confidence in the model. It may be possible to alter some aspects of the model so that it accounts for the new evidence. Bogus science typically invents models that are not falsifiable and then works on finding confirmations. * The luminiferous aether model was falsifiable and has been falsified. The model is not falsifiable because there is no way we can receive information from any other universe. Reincarnation is not a scientific model. * The biological evolutionary model is falsifiable – as explained above – but has not been falsified. * The Intelligent Design model for the existence of the universe is not scientific because it is not falsifiable. A model can be falsifiable yet still be bogus. « Scientific models are tested by making predictions and checking them against real world data. Science uses models to explain aspects of the real world.

results.title: Our hypotheses are not just falsifiable; they’re actually false. | Statistical Modeling, Causal Inference, and Social Science
results.content: # Statistical Modeling, Causal Inference, and Social Science. # Our hypotheses are not just falsifiable; they’re actually false. Everybody’s talkin bout Popper, Lakatos, etc. I think they’re great. Falsificationist Bayes, all the way, man! But there’s something we need to be careful about. All the statistical hypotheses we ever make are false. That is, if a hypothesis becomes specific enough to make (probabilistic) predictions, we know that with enough data we will be able to falsify it. So, here’s the paradox. We learn by falsifying hypotheses, but we know ahead of time that our hypotheses are false. The answer is that *the purpose of falsification is not to falsify*. Falsification is useful not in telling us that a hypothesis is false—we already knew that!—but rather in telling us the directions in which it is lacking, which points us ultimately to improvements in our model. Conversely, *lack* of falsification is also useful in telling us that our available data are not rich enough to go beyond the model we are currently fitting. **P.S.** I was motivated to write this after seeing this quotation: “. this article pits two macrotheories . against each other in competing, falsifiable hypothesis tests . . .”, pointed to me by Kevin Lewis. And, no, I don’t think it’s in general a good idea to pit theories against each other in competing hypothesis tests. Instead I’d prefer to embed the two theories into a larger model that includes both of them. I think the whole attitude of A-or-B-but-not-both is mistaken; for more on this point, see for example the discussion on page 962 of this review article from a few years ago.
